memories.text: You are an engineer moving into machine learning from a web background, and you learn best from code before maths.
You want derivations shown before intuition, not after.
Explaining in Hinglish is fine when tutoring, but flashcards should stay in English.
You study in the evening, usually about forty-five minutes at a time.
The Machine Learning Specialisation is your main course.
You prefer plain numpy over frameworks while you are still learning the fundamentals.
You want to implement backpropagation from scratch in numpy without looking anything up.
You are aiming to finish Course 1 before the end of March.
You use m for the number of training examples and n for the number of features.
You write vectors as column vectors, so the design matrix X is shaped (n, m) rather than (m, n).
You use w and b for parameters rather than theta.
You always print array shapes before trying to debug the maths.
You understand gradient descent as repeatedly stepping opposite the gradient until the cost stops falling.
You settled on thinking of the learning rate as the step size, where too large a value overshoots the minimum.
Logistic regression clicked once you saw the sigmoid as squashing a linear score into a probability.
You read the logistic cost as log loss, which penalises confident wrong answers heavily.
Backpropagation finally made sense as the chain rule applied in reverse through the computation graph.
You see the softmax as normalising logits into a distribution that sums to one.
Vectorisation clicked when you replaced the loop over training examples with a single matrix multiply.
You understand regularisation as penalising large weights so the model stops fitting noise.
Feature scaling matters because gradient descent zig-zags when features have very different ranges.
You think of a neural network layer as a linear map followed by a nonlinearity.
Overfitting became concrete when your training loss kept falling while validation loss rose.
You read the derivative of ReLU as one for positive inputs and zero otherwise.
The normal equation gives a closed form solution but is impractical for large n because of the matrix inverse.
The sigmoid saturates for large inputs, which is why gradients vanish in deep stacks.
You realised a perceptron is logistic regression with a step function instead of a sigmoid.
You never resolved why the bias term is left out of regularisation while the weights are penalised.
You are still unsure when to reach for cross-entropy rather than mean squared error.
You asked why the derivative of the sigmoid can be written in terms of the sigmoid itself, and never followed it up.
You wanted to check whether batch normalisation is worth it at the scale you are working at.
You still cannot see why the chain rule gives that particular ordering of the matrix multiplications in backpropagation.
You meant to look up why Adam usually converges faster than plain gradient descent.
The 3Blue1Brown neural network series is the video source you keep returning to.
You keep a numpy scratch notebook for testing array shapes before writing the real thing.
The Deep Learning book chapter on feedforward networks is where you go for notation.
You want to get comfortable with Rust ownership and borrowing.
Ownership clicked when you saw that a move invalidates the original binding.
You never worked out when to reach for Rc rather than Arc.
You run cargo clippy before every commit.
